title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text: This guide covers a server deployment (test, staging or production environment) using Docker Compose. For local development on your workstation, refer to Docker Compose - Overview.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
1. 🖥️ Prerequisites
This guide assumes Git and Docker (with the Compose plugin) are already installed on the target server.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
2. 👤 Create a Dedicated Application User
Running the stack under a dedicated unprivileged user is strongly recommended.
# Create the user (no login, no password)
sudo adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" crisalid

# Allow it to run Docker commands without sudo
sudo usermod -aG docker crisalid
Create the installation directory and assign ownership:
sudo mkdir -p /opt/crisalid
sudo chown -R crisalid:crisalid /opt/crisalid
Switch to the application user for all subsequent steps:
sudo su crisalid
cd /opt/crisalid

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
3. 📥 Clone the Repository
The repository is public — a simple HTTPS clone is sufficient:
git clone https://github.com/CRISalid-esr/crisalid-deployment.git
cd crisalid-deployment

Choose what to deploy
Depending on your context:

Production — deploy from a release tag for a stable, reproducible deployment:
git fetch --tags origin
git switch -c prod/X.Y.Z vX.Y.Z      # e.g. prod/1.5 v1.5.0
Staging / test (stable) — a release tag is also a safe choice here.
Staging / test (latest) — you may prefer to track a branch such as dev-main or a feature branch if you want to follow ongoing development:
git checkout dev-main
git pull origin dev-main

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
4. 🗺️ Multi-Server Deployment (optional)
The stack can be split across two or more servers. A typical split is one server for the data layer and one for the application layer.

Service co-location constraints






Keep Neo4j, IKG, Apollo and Ofelia on the same server




Ofelia schedules tasks using job-exec, which executes commands inside running containers via the Docker daemon. It must share the same Docker host as the containers it targets — in particular IKG.
IKG must be on the same server as Neo4j because offline backups require stopping both services together (see Backup and Restore).
Apollo connects directly to Neo4j and benefits from co-location for latency and simplicity.





Exposing ports between servers
By default, most services only expose ports within the Docker network. When a service on server A needs to reach a service on server B, you must uncomment the relevant ports: section in the corresponding YAML file (e.g. crisalid-bus/crisalid-bus.yaml, neo4j/neo4j.yaml).

Make sure your firewall restricts access to those ports to the other server(s) only.



Preserving local YAML changes across updates
If you have uncommitted changes to compose YAML files (e.g. uncommented ports: sections), use git stash to preserve them when pulling a new version:
git stash push
git fetch --tags origin
git switch -c prod/X.Y.Z vX.Y.Z
git stash pop
Resolve any conflicts that arise after the stash pop before restarting the stack.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
5. 📄 Create .env Files
All configuration is done through .env files. Each component directory under docker/ has a .env.sample to start from.
cd /opt/crisalid/crisalid-deployment/docker/

cp .env.sample .env
cp crisalid-bus/.env.sample  crisalid-bus/.env
cp neo4j/.env.sample         neo4j/.env
cp apollo/.env.sample        apollo/.env
cp cdb/.env.sample           cdb/.env
cp harvester/.env.sample     harvester/.env
cp ikg/.env.sample           ikg/.env
cp sovisuplus/.env.sample    sovisuplus/.env
cp keycloak/.env.sample      keycloak/.env
cp ofelia/.env.sample        ofelia/.env
cp cvs/.env.sample           cvs/.env
cp neo4j-mcp/.env.sample     neo4j-mcp/.env

⚠️ All .env files must exist even for services you do not intend to start — Docker Compose requires them for variable resolution.

The root docker/.env holds shared credentials used by multiple services (RabbitMQ, Neo4j, etc.). Review and fill it in before starting any service.
Also copy the RBAC roles sample for SoVisu+:
cp sovisuplus/config/rbac.roles.sample.yaml sovisuplus/config/rbac.roles.yaml

All subsequent docker compose commands in this guide assume you are in the docker/ directory.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
6. 🐰 Start CRISalid Bus (RabbitMQ)
Almost all services depend on the message bus — start it first.

Configure RabbitMQ credentials
Edit the shared .env and set your RabbitMQ username and password:
vim .env

All services currently share a single RabbitMQ user. Consider using per-service users in production.



Generate the RabbitMQ configuration
This script creates the definitions.json file (exchanges, queues, users) embedded into the container at startup:
./configure_crisalid_bus.sh


Start the bus
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  up -d


Verify
Open an SSH tunnel from your local machine:
ssh -N -L 15672:127.0.0.1:15672 youruser@yourserver
Then access the RabbitMQ management UI at http://localhost:15672. All exchanges, queues and bindings should be pre-declared.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
7. 🌾 Start SVP Harvester

Configure credentials
Edit the harvester .env to set database credentials and external API keys (e.g. Scanr):
vim harvester/.env


Initialize the authentication file
If Basic Auth is enabled (default), create the credentials file before the first start:
mkdir -p harvester/auth
echo '{}' > harvester/auth/users.json
chmod a+wr harvester/auth/users.json


Start
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  up -d


Create the first user
docker exec -it harvester-ui python scripts/add_basic_user.py admin


Verify
ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 youruser@yourserver

UI: http://localhost:8000/admin
Swagger: http://localhost:8000/docs

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
8. 🗄️ Start Neo4j

Configure credentials and memory
Edit the root .env to set Neo4j credentials and, if needed, memory allocation parameters:
vim .env

Check docker/neo4j/neo4j.yaml for options to enable/disable authentication and to expose (or not) the HTTP (7474) and Bolt (7687) ports on the host. Note that the Neo4j UI needs both ports — exposing only HTTP (7474) without Bolt (7687) will show the interface but prevent any query from running.



Start
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile neo4j \
  up -d


Verify
ssh -N -L 7474:127.0.0.1:7474 youruser@yourserver
ssh -N -L 7687:127.0.0.1:7687 youruser@yourserver
Access the Neo4j Browser at http://localhost:7474.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
9. 🔗 Start IKG
IKG is the Python microservice that manages the knowledge graph.

Configure
Edit ikg/.env — the two main variables are:

REFRESH_ORG_REGISTRY: if true, the organizational registry is reloaded from the open data source at every startup (slow). Set to false after the first run and re-enable periodically.
HARVESTERS: the list of harvesters IKG may query. Remove scopus if your institution has no subscription.

You can also choose to not expose port 8001 on the host (it only serves the Swagger UI and a health-check REST endpoint; actual data flows through RabbitMQ or Apollo/GraphQL).


Before the first start
Download the OpenAlex snapshot data so IKG can build the classification tree in Neo4j at startup — see Download the OpenAlex Classification Tree for full details.
bash docker/scripts/download_openalex_tree.sh



Start
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg \
  up -d


Verify
If port 8001 is exposed:
ssh -N -L 8001:127.0.0.1:8001 youruser@yourserver
Test the health route in the Swagger at http://localhost:8001/docs.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
10. 🌬️ Start CDB (Airflow — CRISalid Directory Bridge)

Configure
Edit the root .env to set LDAP parameters (if applicable) and Airflow admin credentials:
vim .env


Add data files
Place your institution’s data files in the CDB data directory:
mkdir -p /opt/crisalid/crisalid-deployment/docker/cdb/data
# copy your files, e.g.:
# cp structures.csv /opt/crisalid/crisalid-deployment/docker/cdb/data/
# cp people.csv     /opt/crisalid/crisalid-deployment/docker/cdb/data/
Data format documentation (French):

Structures
Researchers



Generate the Airflow configuration
./configure_cdb.sh prod

This script overwrites the Airflow .env file. Re-run it whenever the root .env changes.



Start
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg \
  --profile cdb \
  up -d

If you are using local PostgreSQL containers for CDB, add -f docker-compose.local-postgres.yaml and --profile cdb-db. See Docker Compose - Overview for details.



Verify
ssh -N -L 8081:127.0.0.1:8081 youruser@yourserver
Access the Airflow UI at http://localhost:8081.

Enable the broadcast_entities DAG (toggle the on/off switch).
Then enable either load_ldap_structures or load_spreadsheet_structures depending on your setup.


Start with structures only at this stage — loading people triggers publication harvesting and has cascading effects on downstream services.


Troubleshooting: proxy-related pip failures






Corporate proxy — pip install may fail



On servers behind a corporate HTTP proxy, Airflow containers may fail to install their additional Python dependencies at startup with errors such as:
ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement pika==1.3.2
You may encounter other undocumented proxy-related issues not covered here.
Workaround: pre-download the wheels on a machine with direct internet access and serve them as a local directory:
mkdir vendor
pip download -d vendor --only-binary=:all: pika==1.3.2 deepdiff==7.0.1 ldap3==2.9.1
Then in cdb/.env, switch to offline install:
ADDITIONAL_LIBRARIES=--no-index --find-links /opt/vendor pika==1.3.2 deepdiff==7.0.1 ldap3==2.9.1
And in cdb/cdb.yaml, add the vendor directory as a read-only volume:
- ${AIRFLOW_PROJ_DIR:-.}/vendor:/opt/vendor:ro

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
11. 🚀 Start Apollo (GraphQL API)

Configure
Set an API key for SoVisu+ in the root .env:
vim .env   # set SOVISUPLUS_GRAPHQL_API_KEY


Start
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg \
  --profile cdb \
  --profile apollo \
  up -d


Verify
ssh -N -L 4000:127.0.0.1:4000 youruser@yourserver
Access the Apollo Sandbox at http://localhost:4000/graphql.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
12. 🔐 Start Keycloak and SoVisu+

Configure
Edit the relevant .env files:
vim .env             # shared: KEYCLOAK_*, SOVISUPLUS_*, NextAuth secret
vim sovisuplus/.env  # SoVisu+-specific settings
vim keycloak/.env    # Keycloak admin credentials and DB config

HTTPS via reverse proxy (recommended)
If Keycloak and SoVisu+ are exposed through a reverse proxy handling TLS termination (recommended for production), use these settings in keycloak/.env:
KEYCLOAK_HTTP_ENABLED=true
KEYCLOAK_HOSTNAME_STRICT_HTTPS=false
KEYCLOAK_HOSTNAME_STRICT_BACKCHANNEL=false

With this setup, server-to-server calls from SoVisu+ to Keycloak (e.g. .well-known discovery) travel over plain HTTP internally, while external traffic is secured by the reverse proxy.

Set the public URLs in the root .env:
KEYCLOAK_SCHEME=https
KEYCLOAK_PORT=443
KEYCLOAK_HOST=your-keycloak-hostname.example.org
KEYCLOAK_REALM=crisalid-inst

SOVISUPLUS_SCHEME=https
SOVISUPLUS_HOST=your-sovisuplus-hostname.example.org
SOVISUPLUS_PORT=443

SOVISUPLUS_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
To generate a NextAuth secret:
openssl rand -base64 32


Custom SoVisu+ theme
Copy and customise the sample theme:
cp -r sovisuplus/theme-sample sovisuplus/theme
# edit theme files to match your institution's branding



Generate Keycloak configuration
./configure_keycloak.sh


Start
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg \
  --profile cdb \
  --profile apollo \
  --profile keycloak \
  --profile sovisuplus \
  up -d

If using local PostgreSQL containers, add -f docker-compose.local-postgres.yaml and the relevant --profile *-db flags.



Verify
Once running, SoVisu+ should be accessible at your configured public URL (via the reverse proxy).

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
13. 🔌 Start Neo4j MCP Toolbox
The Neo4j MCP Toolbox exposes curated Cypher queries as MCP tools, allowing AI agents and LLM-based clients to query the CRISalid knowledge graph in a structured and authenticated way.






Keycloak service accounts required for authenticated access



The toolbox validates incoming JWTs against Keycloak. Each client application that needs access must have a dedicated Keycloak service account. Service account setup is documented in Using CRISalid AI Skills.



Start
The Neo4j MCP Toolbox requires Neo4j and Keycloak to be running.
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg \
  --profile cdb \
  --profile apollo \
  --profile keycloak \
  --profile sovisuplus \
  --profile neo4j-mcp \
  up -d
The toolbox listens on port 5000 inside the Docker network and is reachable by other containers at http://neo4j-mcp:5000. It is not published to the host by default.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
14. ⏰ Configure Ofelia (Scheduler)
Add --profile ofelia to the startup command. See Docker Compose - Overview for full configuration details.

title: Docker Compose - Step by Step
text:
15. 🔄 Updating to a New Version
# Stash local changes (e.g. uncommented ports: sections) before switching
git stash push

# Pull the new tag
git fetch --tags origin
git switch -c prod/X.Y.Z vX.Y.Z

# Restore local changes and resolve any conflicts
git stash pop

# Pull updated images
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus --profile harvester --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg --profile cdb --profile apollo \
  --profile keycloak --profile sovisuplus --profile neo4j-mcp \
  pull --include-deps

# Recreate containers
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile crisalid-bus --profile harvester --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg --profile cdb --profile apollo \
  --profile keycloak --profile sovisuplus --profile neo4j-mcp \
  up -d
To force-recreate a single container without restarting the others:
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile sovisuplus \
  up -d --no-deps --force-recreate sovisuplus

🧭 Back to Docker Compose - Overview

title: Migrate Your Local Dev Instance to TLS/HTTPS
text:
This section guides you through configuring your local development setup to use HTTPS (TLS) for both SoVisu+ and Keycloak. This is required to enable Saml2 authentication.




Run SoVisu+ on https://sovisuplus.local:3000 and Keycloak on https://keycloak.local:8443, ensuring your local machine and applications trust the self-signed certificates.




We use mkcert to create locally trusted certificates, avoiding browser warnings. On Ubuntu, libnss3-tools is required for browser trust.

Install Prerequisites and mkcert:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install libnss3-tools
curl -JLO "[https://dl.filippo.io/mkcert/latest?for=linux/amd64](https://dl.filippo.io/mkcert/latest?for=linux/amd64)"
chmod +x mkcert-v*-linux-amd64
sudo mv mkcert-v*-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/mkcert

Initialize Local Certificate Authority:

mkcert -install

Generate Certificates: Create a directory to store the files and generate a certificate that covers both domains:

The name and location of “local-certs” matters because it will be referenced later.
mkdir -p ~/local-certs
cd ~/local-certs
mkcert sovisuplus.local keycloak.local localhost 127.0.0.1 ::1

Fix Key Permissions for Docker:

The Keycloak container needs read access to the private key.
sudo chmod a+r ~/local-certs/sovisuplus.local+4-key.pem




You need to update several environment variables in your Next.js application’s .env file and the Keycloak Docker configuration.


Update the URLs to reflect the new https scheme and the Keycloak HTTPS port (8443).
# Before (HTTP)
# WS_SCHEME="ws"
# KEYCLOAK_ISSUER="[http://keycloak.local:8080/realms/crisalid-inst](http://keycloak.local:8080/realms/crisalid-inst)"
# KEYCLOAK_PUBLIC_URL="[http://keycloak.local:8080/realms/crisalid-inst](http://keycloak.local:8080/realms/crisalid-inst)"

# After (HTTPS)
WS_SCHEME=wss
KEYCLOAK_ISSUER="[https://keycloak.local:8443/realms/crisalid-inst](https://keycloak.local:8443/realms/crisalid-inst)"
KEYCLOAK_PUBLIC_URL="[https://keycloak.local:8443/realms/crisalid-inst](https://keycloak.local:8443/realms/crisalid-inst)"

# UNCOMMENT THIS LINE to allow the Next.js server (Node.js) to communicate
# with Keycloak without complaining about the self-signed certificate.
NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0



Update the scheme and port for both Keycloak and SoVisu+ to use HTTPS.
# Before
# KEYCLOAK_SCHEME=http
# KEYCLOAK_PORT=8080
# SOVISUPLUS_URL=http://...

# After
KEYCLOAK_SCHEME=https
KEYCLOAK_PORT=8443
SOVISUPLUS_URL=https://...



Ensure the hostname enforcement variables are set correctly for the TLS setup.
# Invert these values from the default/sample:
KEYCLOAK_HTTP_ENABLED=false
KEYCLOAK_HOSTNAME_STRICT_HTTPS=true





To run the Next.js development server over HTTPS, we need to use the --experimental-https flag along with the certificate files you generated. This is done via a dedicated script in package.json.

package.json contains a ‘dev-tls’ script:

"scripts": {
  "dev": "next dev -H sovisuplus.local -p 3000",
  "dev-tls": "next dev --experimental-https --experimental-https-key ~/local-certs/sovisuplus.local+4-key.pem --experimental-https-cert ~/local-certs/sovisuplus.local+4.pem -H sovisuplus.local -p 3000"
}

How ro Run the Dev Server with TLS:

Instead of npm run dev, use:
npm run dev-tls

Reference: This approach uses built-in Next.js functionality. See Vercel KB: Access Next.js localhost HTTPS certificate self-signed.





You must now modify your docker compose environment to start Keycloak with its HTTPS configuration, which is handled via a dedicated keycloak-tls profile.

Destroy the Old DB:

Keycloak will write the old HTTP configuration into its database. It’s safest to destroy the database volume to force a clean, HTTPS-based configuration import.
# Ensure Docker compose is stopped
# Remove the persisted DB volume
sudo rm -rf docker/keycloak/postgres-data

Renew Configuration Script:

Re-run your configuration script to ensure the Keycloak realm file (crisalid-inst.json) contains the new https:// URLs.
Ensure all the environment variables are set correctly before running the script (step 2).
./configure_keycloak.sh

Update KEYCLOAK_INTERNAL_HOST in docker/.env:

Services that call Keycloak internally (neo4j-mcp, crisalid-agents, sovisuplus) resolve it by its container name. When switching to the TLS profile, update this variable so they target the correct container:
# docker/.env
KEYCLOAK_INTERNAL_HOST=keycloak-tls
The default value is keycloak (plain HTTP profile). Forgetting this change will cause internal token requests to fail with a connection error.

Launch Docker Compose with the TLS Profile:

Replace --profile keycloak with the dedicated --profile keycloak-tls when starting Docker Compose.
docker compose \
  # ... all other profiles ...
  --profile keycloak-tls \ 
  --profile sovisuplus-db \
  up --remove-orphans



Keycloak: Should be accessible securely at https://keycloak.local:844.
SoVisu+: Should be accessible securely at https://sovisuplus.local:3000.

title: Export Keycloak Realm
text:
To update the Keycloak configuration template in this repository, you need to export the current realm from your running Keycloak instance. This guide walks you through exporting the crisalid-inst realm.





The Keycloak service must be running and accessible via Docker Compose.
The realm you wish to export must be named crisalid-inst.





Follow these steps to extract the realm configuration (clients, roles, and settings) from the running container and save it to your local configuration folder (docker/keycloak/config).


Connect to your running Keycloak service container via the terminal:
docker exec -it keycloak /bin/bash



Inside the container, use kc.sh export to create the realm file. We specify --users skip to ensure the export only includes configuration metadata, not specific user data.
/opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh export \
  --dir /opt/keycloak/data/export \
  --realm crisalid-inst \
  --users skip
A file named crisalid-inst-realm.json is created in the container’s export folder.



Exit the container, and run the following command on your host machine to copy the file into your local configuration directory:
From docker/keycloak directory, run:
mkdir -p realm-export # or whatever folder you want to use
docker cp keycloak:/opt/keycloak/data/export/crisalid-inst-realm.json ./realm-export/

Result: You now have the exported realm file at docker/keycloak/realm-export/crisalid-inst-realm.json. You can use this file to update your configuration template located at docker/keycloak/config/crisalid-inst.json.template.

title: Using Docker Compose as Backend for Local Development
text:
This section explains how to use the Docker Compose stack strictly as a backend while running SoVisu+ locally  (Next.js dev server) for frontend development.




Run all shared services (Neo4j, message bus, Keycloak, APIs, databases) in Docker, but run SoVisu+ on your host machine. To make this work, you must:

Map the necessary service ports from containers to the host.
Use a dedicated profile (e.g. sovisuplus-db) to start only SoVisu+ backend services.
Point your local SoVisu+ to these services via env vars and /etc/hosts.





Add these entries to your /etc/hosts (if not already done in the main guide):
127.0.0.1 sovisuplus.local
127.0.0.1 keycloak.local

SoVisu+ uses ORCID OAuth, which requires valid hostnames even for sandbox keys.





You’ll run SoVisu+ locally, so your host needs to reach the containers. Make sure the following port mappings are enabled.


Uncomment the ports section so Postgres is reachable from your host:


sovisuplus.yaml

services:
  svp-db:
    # Overriden by environment specific YAML configurations (e.g. docker-compose.dev.yaml)
    # image: postgres:16
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${SVP_DB_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${SVP_DB_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${SVP_DB_NAME}
    expose:
      - 5432
    #    ports:
    #      - 5432:5432
    volumes:
      - ./postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - svp-network
    healthcheck:
      test: [ 'CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -d ${SVP_DB_NAME} -U ${SVP_DB_USER}' ]
      interval: 1s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
    command: [ "postgres","-c","max_connections=400","-c","superuser_reserved_connections=3" ]
    profiles:
      - sovisuplus-db

  sovisuplus:
    # Overriden by environment specific YAML configurations (e.g. docker-compose.dev.yaml)
    # image: crisalidesr/sovisuplus:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - ${SVP_PORT:-3000}:3000
      - ${SVP_WS_INTERNAL_PORT:-3001}:3001
    environment:
      - INIT_ROLES_ON_START=true
      - RBAC_ROLES_FILE=/config/rbac.roles.yaml
      - DB_HOST=${SVP_DB_HOST:-svp-db}
      - DB_NAME=${SVP_DB_NAME}
      - DB_USER=${SVP_DB_USER}
      - DB_PASSWORD=${SVP_DB_PASSWORD}
      - DB_PORT=${SVP_DB_PORT:-5432}
      - APP_URL=${SOVISUPLUS_URL}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=${SOVISUPLUS_URL}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_SCHEME=${SVP_WS_SCHEME}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_HOST=${SVP_WS_HOST}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_PORT=${SVP_WS_PORT}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_PATH=${SVP_WS_PATH}
      - NEXTAUTH_URL=${SOVISUPLUS_URL}/api/auth
      - NEXTAUTH_SECRET=${NEXTAUTH_SECRET}
      - JWT_TOKEN_EXPIRATION_HOURS=${JWT_TOKEN_EXPIRATION_HOURS:-12}
      - AMQP_HOST=${CRISALID_BUS_HOST:-crisalid-bus}
      - AMQP_PORT=${CRISALID_BUS_AMQP_PORT}
      - AMQP_USER=${CRISALID_BUS_USER}
      - AMQP_PASSWORD=${CRISALID_BUS_PASSWORD}
      - AMQP_QUEUE_NAME=${SVP_AMQP_QUEUE_NAME}
      - AMQP_EXCHANGE_NAME=${SVP_AMQP_EXCHANGE_NAME}
      - GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT_ENABLED=${GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT_ENABLED}
      - GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT_URL=http://${APOLLO_HOST:-apollo}:${APOLLO_API_PORT}/graphql
      - GRAPHQL_API_KEY_ENABLED=${APOLLO_ENABLE_API_KEYS}
      - GRAPHQL_API_KEY=${SOVISUPLUS_GRAPHQL_API_KEY}
      - KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID=${SOVISUPLUS_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID}
      - KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=${SOVISUPLUS_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET}
      - KEYCLOAK_PUBLIC_ADDR=${KEYCLOAK_SCHEME}://${KEYCLOAK_HOST}:${KEYCLOAK_PORT}
      - KEYCLOAK_INTERNAL_ADDR=http://${KEYCLOAK_INTERNAL_HOST}:8080
      - KEYCLOAK_REALM=${KEYCLOAK_REALM}
      - ORCID_URL=${ORCID_URL}
      - ORCID_SCOPES=${ORCID_SCOPES}
      - ORCID_CLIENT_ID=${ORCID_CLIENT_ID}
      - ORCID_CLIENT_SECRET=${ORCID_CLIENT_SECRET}
      - VOCABS_URL=${CRISALID_VOCAB_SEARCH_URL}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_AVAILABLE_VOCABS=${CRISALID_VOCAB_SEARCH_AVAILABLE_VOCABS:-jel,aat,acm,elsst,pactols,euroscivoc}
      - PERSPECTIVE_ROLES_FILTER=${PERSPECTIVE_ROLES_FILTER}
      - PUBLICATION_LIST_ROLES_FILTER=${PUBLICATION_LIST_ROLES_FILTER}
      - DEFAULT_SELF_SCOPED_ROLES=${DEFAULT_SELF_SCOPED_ROLES}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_INSTITUTION_NAME=${INSTITUTION_NAME}
      - FIELD_ENC_PRIMARY_KID=${FIELD_ENC_PRIMARY_KID}
      - FIELD_ENC_KEYS_JSON=${FIELD_ENC_KEYS_JSON}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_WARN_MISSING_IDENTIFIER_TYPES=${SVP_WARN_MISSING_IDENTIFIER_TYPES}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPPORT_SERVICE_EMAIL_ADDR=${SVP_MAINTENANCE_MAIL_ADDRESS}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_ABOUT_PAGE_URL=${SVP_ABOUT_PAGE_URL}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_TERMS_PAGE_URL=${SVP_TERMS_PAGE_URL}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_COMMUNITY_PAGE_URL=${SVP_COMMUNITY_PAGE_URL}
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_HELP_URL=${SVP_HELP_URL}
    depends_on:
      crisalid-bus:
        condition: service_healthy
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config:ro
      - ./theme:/custom-theme:ro
    networks:
      - svp-network
      - crisalid-front
    profiles:
      - sovisuplus

networks:
  svp-network:
    driver: bridge
  crisalid-front:
    driver: bridge

services:
  svp-db:
    image: postgres:16
    container_name: svp-db
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${SVP_DB_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${SVP_DB_PASSWORD}

      - 5432

services:

    # Overriden by environment specific YAML configurations (e.g. docker-compose.dev.yaml)
    # image: crisalidesr/crisalid-apollo:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - ${APOLLO_API_PORT}:4000
    depends_on:
      neo4j:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      # Overriden by environment specific YAML configurations (e.g. docker-compose.dev.yaml)
      # - APP_ENV=DEV
      - NEO4J_URI=bolt://${NEO4J_HOST}:${NEO4J_BOLT_PORT}
      - NEO4J_USER=${NEO4J_USER}
      - NEO4J_PASSWORD=${NEO4J_PASSWORD}
      - ENABLE_API_KEYS=${APOLLO_ENABLE_API_KEYS}
      - API_KEYS=${SOVISUPLUS_GRAPHQL_API_KEY}
    networks:
      - ikg-network
      - crisalid-front
    profiles:
      - apollo

  ikg-network:
    driver: bridge
  crisalid-front:
    driver: bridge

services:
  apollo:
    image: crisalidesr/crisalid-apollo:latest
    ports:
      - ${APOLLO_API_PORT}:4000

Your local SoVisu+ will call http://localhost:${APOLLO_API_PORT} (GraphQL endpoint /graphql).




Only the management UI port is exposed by default, but you can uncomment the AMQP port to allow external tools to connect:


crisalid-bus.yaml

services:
  crisalid-bus:
    # Overriden by environment specific YAML configurations (e.g. docker-compose.dev.yaml)
    # image: rabbitmq:3-management
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER=${CRISALID_BUS_USER}
      - RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS=${CRISALID_BUS_PASSWORD}
      - RABBITMQ_SERVER_ADDITIONAL_ERL_ARGS=-rabbit load_definitions "${CRISALID_BUS_DEFINITIONS_FILE}"
    ports:
      - "${CRISALID_BUS_HTTP_PORT}:15672"
    # - "${CRISALID_BUS_AMQP_PORT}:5672" # To connect app under development on host machine or from external server
    expose:
      - "${CRISALID_BUS_AMQP_PORT}"
    volumes:
      - ./rabbitmq-data:/var/lib/rabbitmq
      - ./rabbitmq-logs/:/var/log/rabbitmq
      - ./definitions.json:${CRISALID_BUS_DEFINITIONS_FILE}:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: rabbitmq-diagnostics check_port_connectivity
      interval: 1s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      - crisalid-front
      - crisalid-back
    profiles:
      - crisalid-bus
networks:
  crisalid-front:
    driver: bridge
  crisalid-back:
    driver: bridge

services:
  crisalid-bus:
    image: rabbitmq:3-management
    container_name: 'crisalid-bus'
    environment:
      - RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER=${CRISALID_BUS_USER}
      - RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS=${CRISALID_BUS_PASSWORD}
      - RABBITMQ_SERVER_ADDITIONAL_ERL_ARGS=-rabbit load_definitions "${CRISALID_BUS_DEFINITIONS_FILE}"
    ports:
      - "${CRISALID_BUS_HTTP_PORT}:15672"
      - "${CRISALID_BUS_AMQP_PORT}:5672"
    expose:
      - "${CRISALID_BUS_AMQP_PORT}"





Replace the sovisuplus profile with sovisuplus-db, which starts the DB and related services but not the SoVisu+ container itself.
Example command:

  --profile cdb \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile apollo \
  --profile crisalid-bus \
  --profile harvester \
  --profile ikg \
  --profile keycloak \
  --profile sovisuplus-db \
  up --remove-orphans

npm run dev:listener # for the backend listener

title: Using CRISalid AI Skills
text:
The Neo4j MCP Toolbox exposes curated Cypher queries as MCP tools, making it easy to integrate structured CRISalid knowledge graph data into LLM-based agents and workflows.
Two toolsets are available:







Toolset
Tools




crisalid-restricted
get-crisalid-schema, list-person-publications


crisalid-unrestricted
above + execute-cypher-readonly



All tools in the restricted toolset require a valid JWT — clients must authenticate via a Keycloak service account.


1. Expose the Toolbox Port on the Host
By default, the neo4j-mcp service only exposes port 5000 inside the Docker network. Other containers (e.g. an LLM agent running in the same stack) can reach it at http://neo4j-mcp:5000 without any extra configuration.
To access the toolbox from the host machine (e.g. during development or from an external client), uncomment the ports: section in docker/neo4j-mcp/neo4j-mcp.yaml:
# ports:
#   - "5000:5000"
Then restart the service:
docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yaml \
  -f docker-compose.prod.yaml \
  --profile neo4j-mcp \
  up -d --no-deps --force-recreate neo4j-mcp
The toolbox will then be reachable at http://localhost:5000 on the host.



2. Create a Keycloak Service Account






Important



Each client application that calls the MCP toolbox needs its own dedicated Keycloak service account. The steps below create one example account — repeat them for every client.



Step 1 — Create the client
In Keycloak admin → Clients → Create client.
Set Client type to OpenID Connect and choose a Client ID (e.g. example-mcp-client):



Step 2 — Configure capabilities
On the next screen (Capability config):

Enable Client authentication
Check Service account roles only — uncheck Standard flow and Direct access grants




Step 3 — Add an Audience mapper
The toolbox validates the JWT aud claim against the fixed value crisalid-graph-mcp. By default Keycloak does not include this in the token — you must add a mapper.
Navigate to: Clients → your client → Client scopes → click the dedicated scope (<client-id>-dedicated) → Add mapper → Configure a new mapper → Audience.
Fill in the mapper as shown:

Name: mcp-example-client-audience
Included Custom Audience: crisalid-graph-mcp
Add to access token: On




Step 4 — Note the client secret
Go to Clients → your client → Credentials and copy the secret. You will pass it as KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET in your client environment.




3. Example Client (Python)
Install the dependency:
pip install toolbox-langchain
# or with uv:
uv add toolbox-langchain
The following example connects to the toolbox, authenticates against Keycloak using the client_credentials grant, and loads the restricted toolset:
import asyncio
import os

import httpx
from toolbox_core.protocol import Protocol
from toolbox_langchain import ToolboxClient

TOOLBOX_URL = "http://localhost:5000"  # adjust if running inside the Docker network
KEYCLOAK_ISSUER = os.environ["KEYCLOAK_ISSUER"]        # e.g. https://keycloak.example.org/realms/crisalid-inst
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID = os.environ["KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID"]  # e.g. example-mcp-client
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET = os.environ["KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET"]


def get_token() -> str:
    response = httpx.post(
        f"{KEYCLOAK_ISSUER}/protocol/openid-connect/token",
        data={
            "grant_type": "client_credentials",
            "client_id": KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID,
            "client_secret": KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET,
        },
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()["access_token"]


async def main():
    async with ToolboxClient(TOOLBOX_URL, protocol=Protocol.MCP_LATEST) as toolbox:
        tools = await toolbox.aload_toolset(
            "crisalid-restricted",
            auth_token_getters={"crisalid-keycloak": get_token},
        )
        print(f"Loaded {len(tools)} tool(s): {[t.name for t in tools]}")

        schema_tool = next(t for t in tools if t.name == "get-crisalid-schema")
        result = await schema_tool.ainvoke({})
        print(result)


asyncio.run(main())






Note



Protocol.MCP_LATEST is required — toolbox v1.1.0 and above enforce the MCP protocol version on the client handshake.


The toolset name passed to aload_toolset() must match one of the toolsets served by the toolbox (crisalid-restricted or crisalid-unrestricted). The auth token getter key (crisalid-keycloak) must match the auth service name configured in the toolbox.

title: Semantic Embeddings
text:
Embedding vectors are used by two services in the CRISalid AI stack:
Both services use the same embedding endpoint and model — configured once in the shared .env.

title: Semantic Embeddings
text:
Shared configuration
The following variables are shared by IKG and CRISalid Agents. Set them in the common .env file:
EMBEDDING_API_URL=https://your-embedding-server/
EMBEDDING_API_KEY=<your-api-key>
EMBEDDING_API_MODEL=<model-name>
EMBEDDING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=30
Only the openai_compatible provider is supported in Docker Compose deployments. It connects to any remote HTTP service exposing a /v1/embeddings endpoint (OpenAI, vLLM, Hugging Face TEI, or any compatible API).






Recommended provider: ILaaS



ILaaS offers a sovereign French embedding API that works out of the box with the openai_compatible provider. It is the recommended choice for institutions subject to French or European data sovereignty requirements.
With ILaaS and the bge-m3 model (strong multilingual performance on academic French and English):
EMBEDDING_API_URL=https://rag-api.ilaas.fr
EMBEDDING_API_KEY=<your-ilaas-api-key>
EMBEDDING_API_MODEL=bge-m3
EMBEDDING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=30

title: Semantic Embeddings
text:
IKG-specific configuration
The following variables are specific to IKG and are set in docker/ikg/.env:
# Enable batch embedding computation in the IKG service (default: false)
EMBEDDING_ENABLED=true

# Must match the model's actual output size; used to configure the Neo4j vector index.
# Common values: 384 (multilingual-e5-small), 768 (e5-base), 1024 (bge-m3), 1536 (OpenAI ada-002)
EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS=1024

# Number of texts sent per request. Must not exceed the server's max-client-batch-size.
EMBEDDING_BATCH_SIZE=32

title: Semantic Embeddings
text:
Computing embeddings (IKG)
Once enabled, embeddings are updated automatically after each write that produces embeddable nodes. For an existing graph, or to reprocess failed nodes, run the CLI inside the running container:
# Process all pending and failed nodes (default)
docker compose exec crisalid-ikg python -m app.cli literals compute-embeddings

# Restrict to specific literal types (e.g. titles and abstracts only)
docker compose exec crisalid-ikg python -m app.cli literals compute-embeddings \
  --types document_title,document_abstract
The command prints status counts before and after:
Embedding status counts: {'pending': 42831, 'success': 0}
...
Done. Embedding status counts after: {'success': 42831}

title: Semantic Embeddings
text:
Changing the embedding model
If you switch to a model with a different output dimension, update EMBEDDING_API_MODEL in the common .env and EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS in docker/ikg/.env, restart the stack, then rebuild the vector index:
docker compose exec crisalid-ikg python -m app.cli literals compute-embeddings \
  --recreate-vector-indexes






Warning



--recreate-vector-indexes resets all embeddings and recomputes them from scratch. The graph remains usable during reprocessing; vector search results will be partial until all nodes are processed.

A knowledge graph offers the same benefits as a vector store — embedding-based retrieval, semantic search — but goes further. A traditional RAG can answer questions such as:

More broadly, this approach opens the way to conversational analytics — providing actionable insights through natural language, without the heavy business intelligence tooling and specialist skills traditionally required.

title: Introduction
text:
Architecture
Crisalid AI consists of four layers, from the user interface down to the knowledge graph:





flowchart LR
    UI["🖥️ User Interface<br/>OpenWebUI · email · …"]
    AGENTS["🤖 Crisalid Agents<br/>OpenWebUI Pipelines<br/>LangChain · LangGraph"]
    SKILLS["🛠️ Crisalid AI Skills<br/>MCP Tools"]
    GRAPH["🕸️ Neo4j Graph<br/>(IKG)"]

    UI --> AGENTS --> SKILLS --> GRAPH







Why a layered architecture?
Separating concerns across layers maximises reuse and flexibility:

A Crisalid AI Skills tool can be used both in a long-running production agent and in a one-off agent created for a limited trial with a business service.
A Crisalid Agents agent can be developed exploratively using LangChain whilst benefiting from the full Crisalid AI ecosystem.
Other user interfaces may be added in the future: alternative chat solutions (LibreChat), or email and workflow tools such as N8N.

title: Introduction
text:
Layers

🕸️ The graph layer
The Neo4j graph is powered by the IKG middleware. IKG is not part of the Crisalid AI stack — it is a prerequisite to build the graph (see Crisalid Core).


🛠️ The tools layer
The crisalid-ai-skills repository brings together the tool technologies that enable access to the graph, whether via MCP, skills, or non-standard approaches.
The current implementation uses the Neo4j MCP Toolbox (documentation).
Two toolsets are available:







Toolset
Description




crisalid-restricted
A small set of tools with pre-prepared Cypher queries


crisalid-unrestricted
All of the above, plus the ability to execute any read-only Cypher query









Important



With Neo4j Community Edition, role-based access control (RBAC) is not available. The crisalid-unrestricted toolset is therefore a sensitive option that should be reserved for agents requiring elevated authorisation.




🤖 The agent layer
The agent layer enables the development of agents within the LangChain–LangGraph ecosystem, leveraging the full Crisalid AI stack.
Currently, two general-purpose agents have been developed:

Active — a LangGraph-based agent using Crisalid AI Skills tools.
Disabled — an agent based on direct LangChain Neo4j integration, currently inactive due to disappointing performance.

More specialised agents may be developed in the future.
Crisalid Agents also includes OpenWebUI Pipelines, enabling LangGraph agents to be deployed directly from OpenWebUI.


🖥️ The interface layer
For the time being, this consists solely of OpenWebUI — a self-hosted chat interface accessible via a web browser.
The LangChain/LangGraph agents in Crisalid Agents are presented to the user as pipelines — in the place where the user would normally select LLMs in a basic use of OpenWebUI.






Note



Although the user no longer interacts directly with the LLMs, OpenWebUI still needs direct access to the models for convenience features such as generating titles, follow-up questions, etc.

title: Security
text:
Exposure risk



Exposing Crisalid AI on the web without proper security puts you at risk of:

Data leaks — institutional or personal data from the knowledge graph accessible to unauthorised users
LLM exhaustion — uncontrolled consumption of tokens, which is critical with pay-per-token or quota-limited providers
Crisalid AI’s four-layer architecture means that security must be configured at each layer independently. The sections below cover each layer from the graph up.

title: Security
text:
🕸️ The graph layer — Neo4j
Neo4j is secured by a username and password, configured in docker/neo4j/.env.






No RBAC in Neo4j Community Edition



Neo4j Community Edition does not support role-based access control (RBAC). All authenticated users have the same level of access to the graph. For fine-grained access control, the Enterprise Edition is required.
In a Community Edition deployment, the choice of toolset (crisalid-restricted vs crisalid-unrestricted) is the primary access control mechanism — see the tools layer below.


In production, avoid storing the Neo4j password in plain-text .env files. Use a sovereign secret management solution such as HashiCorp Vault.

title: Security
text:
🛠️ The tools layer — Neo4j MCP
The Neo4j MCP Toolbox does not support passwords or API keys. Authentication relies exclusively on JWT tokens issued by an OIDC provider — in the Crisalid stack, this is Keycloak.
Each client application (such as crisalid-agents) must be provisioned with a Keycloak service account to obtain tokens. This setup requires the Keycloak component of the Crisalid stack to be deployed and running.






Local workstation



The Keycloak requirement makes MCP toolbox authentication impractical on a local workstation. For local development, leave KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID and KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET empty in docker/crisalid-agents/.env — the toolbox client will then connect without authentication (suitable for a trusted local environment only).


Port 5000 is not exposed on the host — it is only reachable inside the Docker network. See the local workstation page if you need to access it from outside the stack.
For the full Keycloak service account setup procedure, see Using CRISalid AI Skills.

title: Security
section: 🤖 The agent layer — Crisalid Agents (OpenWebUI Pipelines)
text:
🤖 The agent layer — Crisalid Agents (OpenWebUI Pipelines)
OpenWebUI Pipelines exposes a FastAPI server on port 9099. This endpoint is secured by a shared API key (PIPELINES_API_KEY).
The key is set once and must be provided by any client connecting to the pipelines server — in the Crisalid stack, this client is OpenWebUI itself.
In the Docker deployment, the key is configured in the shared docker/.env:
CRISALID_AGENTS_PIPELINES_API_KEY=<your-secret-key>
It is injected into crisalid-agents as PIPELINES_API_KEY — the server uses it to authenticate incoming requests.
When adding the pipelines connection in OpenWebUI (Admin panel → Settings → Connections, URL http://crisalid-agents:9099), enter this key by hand in the API key field.
Port 9099 is not exposed on the host — it is only reachable inside the Docker network (agents-network).

title: Security
text:
🖥️ The interface layer — OpenWebUI
OpenWebUI is the only layer directly exposed to end users.

User registration is disabled (ENABLE_SIGNUP=false) — accounts must be created manually by an administrator.
An admin account is seeded on first run via OPENWEBUI_ADMIN_EMAIL and OPENWEBUI_ADMIN_PASSWORD in docker/openwebui/.env.
Keycloak SSO integration is planned for a future release.

title: Data backup and restoration with Docker Compose
text:
⚡ Quick backup (filesystem copy)

Fast and simple. Suitable for development or emergency copies.


⚠️ This backup method will include both neo4j and system databases, so it will overwrite users/passwords on restore.


Backup
cd docker/neo4j

sudo tar --numeric-owner -czvf neo4j-data-$(date +%F).tar.gz data


Restore

⚠️ Neo4j must be stopped before restoring. It is highly recommended to stop all the services hat are directly speaking to Neo4j (e.g. crisalid-ikg, crisalid-apollo, ofelia, etc.) to avoid any connection issues during the restore process.

cd docker

docker compose --file docker-compose.yml \
  --file docker-compose.dev.yml \
  --profile neo4j \
  --profile ikg \
  --profile apollo \
  --profile ofelia \
  stop neo4j crisalid-ikg apollo crisalid-ofelia
Then:
tar -xzvf neo4j-data-YYYY-MM-DD.tar.gz -C docker/neo4j
Fix ownership:
cd docker/neo4j
sudo chown -R 7474:7474 data
Restart:
docker compose --profile neo4j up -d neo4j
In case you have a direct access to the source server, direct synchronization is possible:
cd docker/neo4j
sudo rsync -avz --delete \
  user@source-server:/path/to/neo4j/data/ \
  data/

title: Data backup and restoration with Docker Compose
text:
🧱 Proper backup (recommended)

Safe backup using neo4j-admin.

Before running the backup script, check your NEO4J_ADMIN_IMAGE variable in .env to ensure you are using the correct Neo4j version for the backup.

Backup (on source environment)
./scripts/neo4j_offline_backup.sh dev
This:

stops Neo4j
dumps databases into neo4j/backups/<timestamp>/
restarts services




Restore (on target environment)

case 1: restore backup on a local development environment. case 2: restore backup into a staging environment (e.g. staging)


Transfer backup directory from production to target machine (using SFTP or equivalent)
Place it in:

docker/neo4j/backups/<timestamp>/
Fix permission issues to allow the restore script to read the dump files:
cd docker/neo4j/backups/<timestamp>/
sudo chown -R 7474:7474 .

Run:

./scripts/neo4j_offline_restore.sh dev <timestamp>

⚠️ Only the neo4j database is restored (not system), so users/passwords are preserved.
crumbs: Data backup and restoration with Docker Compose

title: Data backup and restoration with Docker Compose
text:
Case 1 — PostgreSQL inside Docker Compose
Containers:

svp-db
harvester-db


Backup
Run sovisuplus (at least the database container) in detached mode:
docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml \
                -f docker-compose.dev.yaml \
                -f docker-compose.local-postgres.yaml \
                --profile sovisuplus-db  up -d
Then, dump the database into custom format (compressed, non-plain SQL):
docker compose exec -T svp-db \
  pg_dump -U "$SVP_DB_USER" -d "$SVP_DB_NAME" \
  --format=custom --no-owner --no-privileges \
  > sovisuplus.dump
Run the same commands for Harvester:
docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml \
                -f docker-compose.dev.yaml \
                -f docker-compose.local-postgres.yaml \
                --profile harvester-db  up -d
docker compose exec -T harvester-db \
  pg_dump -U "$HARVESTER_DB_USER" -d "$HARVESTER_DB_NAME" \
  --format=custom --no-owner --no-privileges \
  > harvester.dump



Restore
For the restoration commands to works, the databases container should have be started at least once and the databases initialized by prisma or alembic migrations.
cat sovisuplus.dump | \
  docker compose exec -T svp-db \
  pg_restore -U "$SVP_DB_USER" \
    -d "$SVP_DB_NAME" \
    --clean --if-exists \
    --no-owner --no-privileges
cat harvester.dump | \
  docker compose exec -T harvester-db \
  pg_restore -U "$HARVESTER_DB_USER" -d "$HARVESTER_DB_NAME" \
    --clean --if-exists \

🌍 Environment-specific Compose files (DEV / PROD)
The repository ships with additional Compose files to adapt the same modular stack to different environments:

DEV overlay (docker-compose.dev.yaml)

Docker image tags for components under active development are not pinned (typically :latest).
Environment variables that depend on the environment (e.g. APP_ENV, when present) are set to DEV.

Use the overlays by combining files with -f (the overlay only overrides what differs from the base file).

title: Docker Compose - Overview
text:
🗄️ Local PostgreSQL vs external PostgreSQL
Several CRISalid components can use either:

a local PostgreSQL container managed by Docker Compose
or an external PostgreSQL server already provided by the institution

This is handled with two mechanisms:

the base Compose files are now external-DB compatible by default
the file docker/docker-compose.local-postgres.yaml re-adds the depends_on relationships required when using local PostgreSQL containers


Base principle
For each component:

the application service uses ${..._DB_HOST} and can therefore point either to a local container or to an external host
the local PostgreSQL service is placed in its own dedicated profile
local PostgreSQL startup dependencies are added only through docker/docker-compose.local-postgres.yaml



Dedicated database profiles
The following profiles are used for local PostgreSQL containers:

harvester-db
sovisuplus-db
keycloak-db
cdb-db

When these profiles are not enabled, the corresponding application uses the database host configured in its .env file.

title: Docker Compose - Overview
text:
🧰 Preparation Steps

1. 🧾 .env Files
Each directory under docker/ (e.g. apollo, crisalid-bus, ikg, neo4j, cdb, harvester, …) has its own .env.sample file.

Copy each .env.sample to .env for each directory except cdb (which is configured by the configure_cdb.sh script).
Fill in appropriate values (hostnames, ports, secrets, etc.)
The main docker/.env.sample includes values used by multiple components (like RabbitMQ or Neo4j credentials)


If you plan to connect the CRISalid Directory Bridge (cdb) to your institutional LDAP, make sure to set:
LDAP_HOST=
LDAP_BIND_DN=
LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD=



2. 🔧 Configure CRISalid Bus
This script reads the .env values and generates the RabbitMQ definitions.json file (exchanges, queues, admin user, etc.).
./docker/configure_crisalid_bus.sh


3. 🔧 Configure CRISalid Directory Bridge (CDB)
This script clones the DAGs, generates environment files, and runs the Airflow initialization.
You must specify the target environment:
./docker/configure_cdb.sh dev
or
./docker/configure_cdb.sh prod



4. 🔐 Configure Basic Authentication for SVP Harvester
SVP Harvester supports HTTP Basic authentication for both its web interface and REST API.
Authentication is enabled by default. You control this behavior via the HARVESTER_ENABLE_BASIC_AUTH environment variable in the harvester’s .env file.

Enable / disable authentication
In docker/harvester/.env:
HARVESTER_ENABLE_BASIC_AUTH=true

true (default): all /admin/* and /api/* endpoints are protected
false: authentication is disabled (all endpoints are public)


⚠️ This authentication mechanism is intended for local development and restricted environments. Always use HTTPS if enabling it in production.




Create the first user
User credentials are stored in a local file mounted into the container:
app/auth/users.json
Before starting the container for the first time, ensure that this file exists and is initialized with an empty JSON object:
mkdir -p harvester/auth
echo '{}' > harvester/auth/users.json
Once the harvester-ui container is running, create an initial user :
docker exec -it harvester-ui python scripts/add_basic_user.py admin
You will be prompted to enter and confirm a password.
The credentials take effect immediately; no container restart is required.



Remove a user
To remove an existing user:
docker exec -it harvester-ui python scripts/remove_basic_user.py admin



🔄 Optional: Full reset of Airflow state
By default, the script does NOT wipe Airflow state (DAG history, users, variables, connections, etc.).
If you want to completely reset Airflow (including metadata database and volumes), use:
./docker/configure_cdb.sh dev --reset
You will be prompted to type RESET to confirm.
⚠️ This removes Docker volumes for the CDB profile and permanently deletes:

DAG execution history
Users and passwords
Variables and connections
XCom data

Use with caution

ℹ️ In dev, Airflow GUI admin credentials are initialized from environment variables (default: admin:admin unless overridden in docker/.env).

After running the script, if you intend to use the CSV mode for structures and people (instead of LDAP), place your data files in:
docker/cdb/data/
├── structure.csv
└── people.csv
Sample CSVs:

docker/cdb/dags/data

Full documentation (in French):

Laboratories
Researchers





5. 🌐 Download the OpenAlex Classification Tree
Before starting IKG for the first time, download the OpenAlex snapshot data (domains, fields, subfields, and topics). IKG uses these files to build the classification tree in Neo4j on its first startup, then wipes them automatically.
bash docker/scripts/download_openalex_tree.sh
When IKG starts, it checks the mounted data directory for snapshot files. If files are present, it runs the import (which is idempotent) and then wipes them so they do not trigger a re-import on the next startup. To refresh the tree later, re-run the script and restart IKG.



6. 🔑 Configure Keycloak
Keycloak is handling authentication within the system. Multiple client applications (such as Sovisu+) can share the same authentication realm. To set up Keycloak in this environment, follow these steps:

Global .env Configuration

In the global .env file, you will find the shared Keycloak configuration variables, such as the realm name ( KEYCLOAK_REALM) and the client secrets (SOVISUPLUS_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET). The KEYCLOAK_REALM can be customized ( e.g., crisalid-my-university) for readability.
Example:
KEYCLOAK_REALM=crisalid-inst
SOVISUPLUS_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=MY-SECRET-VALUE

Keycloak Configuration Script

Run the ./configure_keycloak.sh script. This will create the required configuration file from the template ( docker/keycloak/config/crisalid-inst.json.template).

Customizing Keycloak .env Settings

The docker/keycloak/.env.sample file provides the environment settings for Keycloak, such as the admin credentials and database configurations. Copy the sample file to .env and modify the settings as needed.
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN=admin
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin
KEYCLOAK_DB_VENDOR=postgres
KEYCLOAK_DB_HOST=keycloak-db # Only if you are using the local PostgreSQL container for Keycloak. 
# If using an external database, set this to the appropriate hostname or IP address.
KEYCLOAK_DB_PORT=5432
KEYCLOAK_DB_NAME=keycloak
KEYCLOAK_DB_USER=keycloak
KEYCLOAK_DB_PASSWORD=keycloak

Define specific URIs in /etc/hosts

To ensure that Sovisu+ and Keycloak can be accessed correctly, you need to define specific URIs in your /etc/hosts file. This is necessary because Sovisu+ uses OAuth2 with ORCID, which requires a specific hostname even to deliver “sandbox” keys.
# Add these lines to your /etc/hosts file
127.0.0.1 sovisuplus.local
127.0.0.1 keycloak.local


7. SoVisu+ custom themes
SoVisu+ allows you to customize its appearance using themes. You can create your own theme by following these steps:

Copy the sample theme directory:

cp -r sovisuplus/theme-sample sovisuplus/theme

Edit the theme files in sovisuplus/theme to customize text and images according to your institution’s branding.



8. SoVisu+ RBAC Roles File
SoVisu+ comes with a sample RBAC configuration you can customize. Start by copying the sample file and editing it:
cp sovisuplus/config/rbac.roles.sample.yaml sovisuplus/config/rbac.roles.yaml

Edit sovisuplus/config/rbac.roles.yaml to define your roles by grouping permissions (but dont create new permissions, i.e new actions/subjects/fields as they are used in the code).
After any change, the docker startup script will copy the file to the container and re-seed the roles and permissions in database.



9. ⏰ Configure Ofelia (system-wide scheduler)
Ofelia is the scheduler of the whole CRISalid stack. It runs as its own container and periodically triggers tasks for other containers (by running a CLI command or calling an API endpoint).
Ofelia reads a config file and uses the Docker API to:

job-exec: run a command inside an existing container (via docker exec)
job-local: run a command directly inside the Ofelia container itself (typically, a curl command to call an API)
(and job-run: run a one-shot container if needed)

You can find full documentation here:

Docker Hub: https://hub.docker.com/r/mcuadros/ofelia
GitHub repository: https://github.com/mcuadros/ofelia/tree/master

In this deployment, Ofelia is included as its own Docker Compose profile (ofelia) with:

a compose file: docker/ofelia/ofelia.yaml
a scheduler config file template: docker/ofelia/config.ini
a configuration template: docker/ofelia/.env.sample


Create Ofelia .env
In docker/ofelia/, copy the sample file:
cp docker/ofelia/.env.sample docker/ofelia/.env
The sample content is:
CONFIG_FILE_NAME=config.ini
This variable is used only by Docker Compose to choose which config file to mount inside Ofelia. You can later duplicate config.ini under another name (for example config.dev.ini, config.prod.ini, etc.) and switch by changing CONFIG_FILE_NAME in .env without editing the Compose file:
CONFIG_FILE_NAME=config.dev.ini
# or:
# CONFIG_FILE_NAME=config.prod.ini


Define the scheduled jobs in config.ini
The default scheduler configuration file is:
docker/ofelia/config.ini
Example content:
; file: docker/ofelia/config.ini

[job-exec "ikg-fetch-pubs"]
schedule = @every 2m
container = crisalid-ikg
command = python -m app.cli people fetch-publication-random
This declares a job named ikg-fetch-pubs that:

runs every 2 minutes (@every 2m)
uses job-exec: it executes the command inside the running crisalid-ikg container
calls the internal CLI: python -m app.cli people fetch-publication-random



Run Ofelia with Docker Compose
To start the scheduler along with the rest of the stack, include the ofelia profile, for example:
docker compose \
...
  --profile ofelia \
  up -d

text: This page describes how harvesting is triggered and configured in CRISalid, and how responsibilities are split between the IKG and the Harvester microservices.

title: Harvesting Configuration
text:
🌐 Overview
Harvesting is triggered by messages published on the RabbitMQ publications exchange by the IKG (Institutional Knowledge Graph) service. The Harvester UI provides observability only (although it can be used to trigger harvesting requests manually, but only for testing purposes).
The IKG publishes harvesting requests to the RabbitMQ publications exchange.
Each message represents one harvesting job.
Requests can be triggered:

Manually, via IKG CLI tools
Automatically, via Ofelia (Docker Compose) or Kubernetes Jobs / CronJobs (which in turn call IKG CLI tools)

title: Harvesting Configuration
text:
⚙️ Configuration & Execution
Harvesting is configured at two levels:

IKG: decides when harvesting runs and which harvesters are requested
Harvester: defines which harvesters exist and whether they can run


IKG — Requested Harvesters
The HARVESTERS environment variable defines which harvesters are included in harvesting requests published on the publications exchange.

Can be set via:

runtime environment
Docker Compose (e.g. docker/ikg/ikg.yaml)
Kubernetes ConfigMaps

Overrides the default when defined

Default configuration:
[
  "idref",
  "scanr",
  "hal",
  "openalex",
  "scopus"
]

🔗 Defined in the IKG settings (link to GitHub settings file)




Harvester — Available Harvesters
The Harvester service declares available harvesters in:
harvesters.yaml
This file binds harvester identifiers to their implementations.
- name: idref
  module: app.harvesters.idref.idref_harvester_factory
  class: IdrefHarvesterFactory

- name: scanr
  module: app.harvesters.scanr.scanr_harvester_factory
  class: ScanrHarvesterFactory

- name: hal
  module: app.harvesters.hal.hal_harvester_factory
  class: HalHarvesterFactory

- name: openalex
  module: app.harvesters.open_alex.open_alex_harvester_factory
  class: OpenAlexHarvesterFactory

- name: scopus
  module: app.harvesters.scopus.scopus_harvester_factory
  class: ScopusHarvesterFactory
Only harvesters declared in harvesters.yaml can be executed.

title: Harvesting Configuration
text:
🔁 Execution Rules

The IKG publishes a harvesting request on the publications exchange
The message contains:

the type of entity (currently: person only)
a flag indicating whether a reply is expected
a flag for “identifiers safe mode” (if true, the alignment of identifiers is not recorded in the harvesters database)
a list of event types to be reported (e.g. created, updated, deleted, unchanged)
a list of requested harvesters (e.g. idref, scanr, hal, openalex, scopus)
the fields of the entity to be harvested, including a list of identifiers with their types and values :

name : displayed in the Harvester UI but not used for harvesting
identifiers : used to determine which harvesters can run (e.g. openalex requires an ORCID identifier) and to perform the actual harvesting



{
  "type": "person",
  "reply": true,
  "identifiers_safe_mode": false,
  "events": [
    "created",
    "updated",
    "deleted",
    "unchanged"
  ],
  "harvesters": [
    "idref",
    "scanr",
    "hal",
    "openalex",
    "scopus"
  ],
  "fields": {
    "name": "John Doe",
    "identifiers": [
      {
        "type": "orcid",
        "value": "0000-0002-1825-0097"
      },
      {
        "type": "idref",
        "value": "123456789"
      }
    ]
  }
}

For each requested harvester, the Harvester service checks:

if the harvester is declared in harvesters.yaml
if a compatible identifier is present


A harvester is executed only if a suitable identifier is available (e.g. openalex requires an ORCID and will not run with a HAL identifier).

All eligible harvesters are executed in parallel

title: CRISalid Bus – Exchange Map & Message Catalog
section: 🌐 Global Map of Exchanges and Queues
text:
🌐 Global Map of Exchanges and Queues
CRISalid currently relies on several RabbitMQ exchanges to make its services communicate asynchronously.
In crisalid-bus, all exchanges are of type topic and use an “at-least-once” delivery strategy, which means that messages may be delivered more than once in case of failure, and consumers must be designed to handle potential duplicates and be idempotent. Consumers, in turn, must be able to handle the possibility of missing messages (e.g., by carefully processing “unchanged” events or implementing reconciliation mechanisms).
Messages are primarily of two types: events and tasks.

Events represent occurrences or changes in the system (e.g., “a person was created”, “a publication was harvested”). They are typically not acknowledged (i.e., they are fire-and-forget).
Tasks represent work that needs to be done (e.g., “harvest this publication”). They may be acknowledged (i.e., the producer expects a confirmation that the task was received and will be processed).
